results.text:
In a previous reply I made the comparison of brains as analog computers to silicon as digital computers.  My point was that somehow analog computation by transforming continuous values is more power and real-estate efficient than flipping zeros into ones. (Inversion being the basis of all digital computation).  

But then it occurred to me that the entire analog process within a neuron is driven by an electrical current  of protons that drives a molecular turbine that crams a phosphate onto an ADP molecule transforming it into ATP.  

You could think of ATP molecules as little cocked springs that diffuse through a biological system to sites where they are triggered, releasing their stored energy and transforming back into ADP and a phosphate, only to diffuse back to that turbine to be transformed once again.  

Humans transform their body weight of ATP into ADP every day...

But that transformation is a bit flip.  ADP->ATP  ATP->ADP.  

So then my question is: 

Is the bit flipping of digital computation analogous to the flipping of ADP/ATP.  Or is digital computational bit flipping more energy hungry than biological analog computation.

Another way to ask this is: Does the brain compute more with a single ATP/ADP flip, than a digital computer computes with a single bit flip.  

Hmmmm.

results.text:
Who knew that the primary commercial use of space would be computation? Of all the science fiction I have read, I never encountered that particular theme. Now we have multiple serious companies planning to launch tens of thousands of satellites into sun-synchronous orbital shells as computational data centers.

And, of course, Musk wants to build a mass driver on the moon launching millions of satellites to gather power and do computation.

One of the problems with a big context window (e.g. Claude 4.6) is that it remembers too much.  

Yesterday I told it to reduce crap of some files to 8 or less.  It came back and begged to allow a file to remain at 9 since it was "close".  I said, ok for the time being.

Now today, I sent it back to reduce crap in a bunch of files and when it came to that file it remembered and said that it didn't have to do that one because we didn't do it the night before.  

Grumble.

I woke up this morning with an idea for improving the performance of Empire.  It's an entirely different approach for navigating the world map.  I think it'll cut processing time by a significant factor.

The AI doesn't wake up with new ideas like that.  They don't have light bulb moments.  They don't look sideways at a problem and see it from a novel perspective.  

And the insight I'm talking about derives from my deep knowledge of the system itself, and the way computers operate.  

Try as they might, no matter how much they hope, they'll never be rid of us.

results.text:
In the end I think the administration will lose the 4A battle regarding administrative warrants for forcing home entry to detain illegal immigrants with final orders of deportation.  I think they think so too; because they don't appeal the cases that they lose.  It looks like they don't want this issue moving up through the appellate system.  

This may seem like dirty pool.  In reality it's just part of the normal checks and balances of the system.  Every administration does things like this.  For example Biden's student loan forgiveness attempts or Obama's attempts to grant work permits to certain illegal aliens.   (DACA).
